summary: Goserelin acetate is a synthetic GnRH (LHRH) agonist given as a subcutaneous depot implant (3.6 mg every 28 days or 10.8 mg every 12 weeks). Continuous stimulation desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors, suppressing LH/FSH and gonadal sex hormones, which is exploited in prostate cancer, advanced/premenopausal breast cancer, endometriosis and endometrial thinning. An initial surge of sex hormones causes a transient tumor flare and, in prostate cancer, can worsen symptoms or cause spinal cord compression early in treatment.
indications: Palliative treatment of advanced prostate cancer; with radiotherapy and an antiandrogen for locally confined Stage T2b-T4 disease
Advanced (palliative) and stage-specific management of breast cancer in pre/perimenopausal women
Management of endometriosis, including pain relief and reduction of lesions
Endometrial thinning prior to endometrial ablation for dysfunctional uterine bleeding

dosage.n: Consider initial antiandrogen to cover the testosterone flare
Started before and continued during/after radiotherapy

dosage.d: 3.6 mg implant every 28 days for up to 6 months

admin: Administer as a subcutaneous depot implant into the upper abdominal wall using aseptic technique
Use caution inserting in patients with a low BMI or on anticoagulants (injection-site hematoma)
Give the 3.6 mg depot every 28 days or the 10.8 mg depot every 12 weeks; do not interchange formulations inappropriately
In prostate cancer, start an antiandrogen before/with the first dose to blunt the testosterone flare
Confirm the patient is not pregnant before use in women and use a non-hormonal contraceptive during therapy
moa: Goserelin is a potent synthetic decapeptide analog of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH/LHRH). Initial administration transiently stimulates pituitary release of LH and FSH, raising testosterone (men) or estradiol (women) - the cause of tumor flare. With continuous depot exposure, pituitary GnRH receptors are down-regulated and desensitized, suppressing LH/FSH and reducing serum testosterone to castrate levels in men and estradiol to postmenopausal levels in women, depriving hormone-sensitive tumors and endometriotic tissue of stimulation.

absolute: Pregnancy (except for palliative treatment of advanced breast cancer) - can cause fetal harm/loss
Hypersensitivity to goserelin, GnRH or GnRH agonist analogs
relative: Men at risk of spinal cord compression or ureteric obstruction (flare risk)
Patients with risk factors for decreased bone mineral density
monitor: Tumor flare in the first weeks of prostate cancer therapy

preg: Goserelin is contraindicated in pregnancy except when used for palliation of advanced breast cancer; it can cause fetal harm and pregnancy loss. Exclude pregnancy before starting in women and use non-hormonal contraception during treatment and until menses resume.
lact: Use during breastfeeding is not recommended; it is not known whether goserelin is excreted in human milk and there is potential for serious adverse effects in the infant.
renal: No dosage adjustment is required in renal impairment.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is required in hepatic impairment.

major: Drugs that prolong the QT interval / cause Torsades - androgen deprivation may prolong QT; assess risk and monitor ECG/electrolytes
moderate: Antidiabetic agents - androgen/estrogen deprivation can worsen glucose control; may need dose adjustment
minor: Other hormonal therapies - additive endocrine effects (often intentional, e.g. with antiandrogens)
interactions.food: Not applicable - administered as a subcutaneous implant.
interactions.diagnostics: Suppresses gonadotropins and sex steroids; may raise glucose and alter lipids and reduce bone density on DXA. Pituitary gonadotropin/sex-steroid tests are affected during therapy.

common: Vaginal dryness, breast changes, mood changes (women)
serious: Tumor flare with worsening prostate cancer symptoms, ureteric obstruction or spinal cord compression early in therapy
Decreased bone mineral density / osteoporosis with prolonged use
Hyperglycemia and increased risk of diabetes
Cardiovascular events (MI, stroke, sudden death) reported with GnRH agonists
rare: Pituitary apoplexy (rare, usually soon after first dose)
Injection-site hematoma / rarely vascular injury at insertion
emergency: Spinal cord compression or acute urinary obstruction during flare
Pituitary apoplexy (sudden headache, visual changes, altered consciousness)

monitoring: Serum testosterone (men) or estradiol (women) to confirm adequate suppression; PSA in prostate cancer
Symptoms of tumor flare in the first weeks - urinary obstruction, bone pain, neurologic signs (cord compression)
Bone mineral density with long-term therapy
Blood glucose / HbA1c and cardiovascular risk factors; blood pressure
Serum calcium in patients with bony metastases
counsel: This is a small implant placed under the skin of the abdomen on a regular schedule - keep your appointments
Early on, prostate cancer symptoms (bone pain, urinary trouble) may briefly worsen (tumor flare); report worsening pain, leg weakness or trouble urinating urgently
Hot flushes, reduced sexual desire and mood changes are common; long-term use can weaken bones
Women must use non-hormonal birth control and tell their doctor at once if they could be pregnant; report persistent headache or vision changes
pk: Initial hormone surge (flare) in first days; suppression to castrate levels in ~2-4 weeks
Continuous depot release; serum peaks days after implant
Approximately 4-5 hours (longer in renal impairment but no dose change needed)
Sustained suppression over 28 days (3.6 mg) or 12 weeks (10.8 mg)
Store below 25 C; do not freeze
pearls: Tumor flare: the initial LH/testosterone surge can transiently worsen prostate cancer - co-administer an antiandrogen and watch for spinal cord compression and urinary obstruction in high-risk men
Down-regulates pituitary GnRH receptors with continuous dosing, producing medical castration (men) or postmenopausal estradiol levels (women)
Limit endometriosis therapy to ~6 months because of bone mineral density loss
No renal or hepatic dose adjustment needed
Class warnings: reduced bone density, hyperglycemia/diabetes and cardiovascular events with androgen deprivation
missed: Goserelin is given by a clinician on a fixed schedule (every 28 days or every 12 weeks). If an implant is delayed, it should be administered as soon as possible; do not attempt to self-dose. Significant delays can allow hormone levels to rise - contact the treating team to reschedule promptly.
overdose: There is no experience of overdose; if it occurs, management is symptomatic and supportive. Because it is a depot implant, the effect is not rapidly reversible.
